newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end mixed after consumer price data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end mixed after consumer price data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended mixed on Wednesday after the government's September consumer price data matched economists' forecasts, allowing government securities prices to trade in fairly wide, but familiar ranges.

The Labor Department said its Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.3 percent in September and that its core CPI, the CPI without its more volatile food and energy items, also rose a moderate 0.3 percent.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended at 98-19/32, down 7/32, to yield 6.86 percent.

Especially when averaged with the previous month's very slight 0.1 percent gains on the consumer price front, the September CPI report gave the market fresh assurance that inflation, at least outside the wage arena, remained in check and the market staged a brief "relief" rally.
But selling pressure was not far behind.

At mid-morning, the government reported that real earnings rose 0.8 percent in September, following a revised 1.2 percent increase in August. The real earnings report rarely attracts the market attention since it reworks data already disclosed in the monthly employment report and consumer price index.
But this time, the real earnings data managed to arouse the market's fear of potential wage inflation.

"This is a report that has never received close attention in the market and really does not provide any new information," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "It surprises me that it had an influence on the market, but it did seem to have some sway."

"Who would have thought that we would react to real earnings but apparently, the report was one of the catalysts behind the selling pressure," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
Rumors of central bank selling also pushed the market lower during the first half of the session, traders said.

"Buying by central banks has been one of the key elements supporting our market and a rumor of them selling would represent a loss of support for our market," said Moran. "It could be an interesting and important development."
The selling pressure coincided with news that Russia's interior minister had accused security chief Alexander Lebed of plotting to seize power while President Boris Yeltsin awaits heart surgery.

"This was just pent-up selling that had to be done," contended Waldo Best, senior economist at BZW Securities Inc. "The international bond market and central bank buying had been driving the market up during the last few days and they stopped buying. The European markets took a break and that resulted in the U.S. market taking a break as well."
A majority of the day's losses were erased by the end of the session and the market ended mixed.
"We have been on familiar territory for some time and we've just been bouncing around," said Moran. "I don't think anyone has made any major portfolio shifts."

"The market is really rangebound. It's directionless. It's comfortable at these levels," said Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "There's no smoking gun on inflation, the economy seems to be slowing in the third quarter and the Fed is on hold."
Three- and six-month bill rates fell, as did the year bill rate, to five percent, 5.12 percent and 5.27 percent, respectively.

The two-year note ended at 100-5/32, up 1/32, to yield 5.91 percent. Five-year notes ended unchanged at 100-11/32, yielding 6.29 percent. The ten-year note closed at 99-18/32, down 2/32, to yield 6.56 percent. -- 212-859-1679
